<reason>In an exceptionally high-level debate from both sides, Side A wins by executing a superior economic and comparative case across the second half of the exchange. Side A's pressure questions forced Side B to concede in Rebuttal 2 that its replacement mandates would cause owners of existing older rentals not to sell, shifting development only to vacant or commercial lots while relying on rent stabilization to protect sitting tenants. Side A capitalized on this concession in a brilliant closing speech, demonstrating that freezing the existing residential footprint creates chronic vacancy scarcity—the exact condition Side B blamed for making relocation vouchers ineffective—and locks out any working-class family who needs to move or outgrows their current unit. Side B made a strong point on the timing gap between immediate demolition and future supply/tax revenue, keeping the debate competitive, but Side A ultimately proved that the localized short-term risk of by-right redevelopment is far more manageable than the permanent exclusion caused by scarcity.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's pressure question [A3.2] and closing crystallization [A5.1]-[A5.3]: Side A asked why an owner of an existing rental would ever sell if heavy replacement mandates pushed redevelopment value below current use value. When Side B answered in [B4.2] that "the owner would not sell — and that is the point," Side A turned that admission into a decisive critique showing how Side B's model manufactures chronic vacancy scarcity and protects only immobile incumbents.</best_rebuttal>
